en: ie3> Rāmarudrī:
Having bowed at the feet of the Sun, Rāmacandra Tāta, who is like a boat for crossing the forests of the lotuses of logic;

The virtuous Śrī Rāmarudra, for the benefit of the wise, performs some small wonder by the power of his divine play. (1) I know that there is never any other supreme deity here apart from the very nature of Śiva; therefore, this...
Today, because she is a river here, I offer this composition as water for the feet at her two lotus-feet.
May this *Taraṅgiṇī*, with its words of fruitful expression, swiftly bring joy and knowledge to the wise,
and may it ever be sufficient for those adorned by the mass of splendor arising from the fame of the entire vessel of the universe.

3. Mahādeva, desiring to compose a commentary on the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī*, first records at the beginning an auspicious invocation in the form of a salutation to his father—which was performed to remove obstacles to the commencement of the work—for the purpose of instructing his disciples, beginning with the words "Lakṣmī... He then expands upon the hidden meanings.
The meaning is that he causes expansion. "Expansion of the subject matter" (arthavistāra) refers to its connection with various people;
and in the present context, the sense is that this connection pertains specifically to those who possess knowledge concerning its own object.
Regarding the phrase "tatra tāvad": it is a particle used as an ornament for the sentence. The disciples also [understand] thus.
Regarding "they should do so": here, the meaning of the word *iti* (thus) is the intention regarding the aforementioned form [of action].

Since the word *iti* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), its being in the third case-ending results in the sense: "with the intention that the disciples also should act in this manner. By this, the disciples...

The objection that [the word *kuryuḥ*] is inconsistent with the text— on the grounds that knowledge, desire, and verbal expressions of the form "one should do thus" do not constitute instruction to a disciple,

and therefore the phrase "for the instruction of the disciple" (*śiṣyaśikṣāyai*) is inappropriate because the meaning of the word "instruction" (*śikṣā*) is simply the knowledge of one's own duty— is refuted. [This is so] because of the principle of "repetition of what has already occurred" (*samāptapunarāttatvam*).

*Samāptapunarātta* (the resumption of what has already been concluded) is a poetic defect consisting in the re-engagement with a substantive word—whose desire for further qualification has already been satisfied through syntactic connection with a preceding attribute—in order to connect it with another attribute. In the present instance: "He who made the moon his crest-jewel and Vāsuki his bracelet... [and so forth].

In the phrase "May Bhava’s playful cosmic dance (līlātāṇḍava) be for the welfare of the fortunate," the requirement for the word *bhava* is satisfied by the syntactic cognition (*anvayabodha*) that "may Bhava be for the welfare" alone; therefore,
for the sake of connecting it with the specific attribute "playful cosmic dance" occurring later on, [the word *bhava* must be supplied].

The sense is that, in order to satisfy the expectation of what kind of "existence" (bhava) that is, the recollection of existence is necessitated by the word *bhava*; thus, there is the fault of *samāpta-punar-ātta* (resuming what has already been concluded).
Now, [one might object]: "But for words whose grounds for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) are either a genus (*jāti*) or something other than that..."

There is a rule that only a word denoting the qualified object (viśeṣya) has birth and activity as its cause [of its application]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usage as "blue-lotus" (*utpala-nīla*) being equivalent to "lotus-blue" (*nīla-utpala*), just as "blue-lotus" (*nīla-utpala*) is.
For instance, according to the sūtra prescribing compounds, that which is indicated by a word ending in the nominative case becomes the first member in the compound.
The rule is that [the shorter word] falls first. In the sūtra prescribing the *karmadhāraya* compound, "the qualifier by the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*),
because the word expressing the qualifier is indicated as being in the nominative case, there is a rule for its prior placement.
In the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), since there is no restrictive factor determining the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified,

if one intended the lotus to be the qualifier, the usage "lotus-blue" (*utpalanīla*) would indeed be possible; therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that because the word "lotus" has its application based on a genus (*jāti*), it functions exclusively as the denoter of the qualified object.

And thus, since the word *bhava*— which has as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) a specific genus residing in the body of Śiva— is intended to denote a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇaparatva*), it is untenable [to claim otherwise]. Nor is there any inconsistency in the cognition "Bhava knows everything," because the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvarajñāna*) conveys the possession of knowledge through the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*).
Furthermore, it should not be argued that [the term] cannot be accepted as being delimited by itself;

for we admit that the referent of the word *bhava* (existence) is precisely a conscious entity qualified by such a specific universal (*vaijātya*) through the relation of being delimited by its own substratum. And "being delimited by its own substratum" means...

It should be understood that [the definition] consists in being qualified by its own substratum through the relation of possessing an effort which is the uncommon cause of the action residing in itself. Nor should it be argued that *bhavatva* (the state of being) is not a universal (*jāti*) because it possesses only a single individual instance;

for the body of Śiva also differs according to the difference between cosmic cycles (*kalpa*). Nor [should it be argued that it is not a universal] because [the etymology] "from this the world comes into being" [applies].

It must be stated that, due to its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the status of being the cause of the world alone is the basis for the application of the term *bhava*, and not a specific genus (*jāti*);
for it has been said by the most learned that etymological meaning (*yoga*) is more powerful than conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Since the fault of *samāptapunarātta* (resuming what has been concluded) would necessarily arise if one were to adopt the conventional meaning—which is established through rapid presentation—and thereby achieve a comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) free from further expectancy, while failing to adopt the etymological meaning—which involves delayed presentation—at this point he says: "In reality, however... (*vastutastu*).

Regarding the phrase "when there is such an expectation" (*ityākāṅkṣāyām*): the word "being present" (*sati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This means that a comprehension free from expectation is not possible;
that is to say, a verbal cognition in which an expectation has not arisen within one's own [mental] continuum does not occur.

Regarding the phrase "the intended cognition of the syntactic relation" (*vivakṣitānvayabodha*): after the generation of a syntactic cognition that is free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*) by means of the word expressing the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the subsequent mental re-engagement (*anusaṃdhāna*) of that same word expressing the qualificand for the sake of connecting it with another qualifier is what constitutes "resuming what has been concluded" (*samāptapunarātta*). Thus, it is included as a constituent element of the definition of *samāptapunarātta*.
The meaning is that there is an absence of the intended cognition of a syntactic relation free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣānvayabodha*).
By the phrase "if such qualifiers as 'pastime' (*līlā*) and so forth are not stated," it is implied that when such qualifiers are stated,
the resulting cognition of a syntactic relation is indeed one produced by a sentence accompanied by those specific qualifiers.

It has been indicated that the intended cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) occurs. Now, one might object: "In that case, the state of having a completed meaning (*samāptaparatva*) would never be a defect. Since expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the sole determinant for verbal cognition in general, any slight expectancy—such as 'what is it like? and so forth—would suffice for the purpose of connecting it with another qualifier."
Because it is impossible for there to be a cognition free from expectancy anywhere when [the meaning] must be supplied through imagination, he says:
"by means of an expectancy that has been raised. This means by an indefinite expectancy;
for even in the case of words such as "son," the mutual expectancy between words denoting actions and their factors (kriyākāraka) is fixed.

The expectancy for a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) is indeed necessary, and likewise, the expectancy for a purpose (*prayojana*) is also necessarily required, because in the absence of a purpose, the very meaning of the sentence would fail to be established. However, the expectancy such as "of what nature is existence?
is not necessary. Thus, after the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) devoid of such necessary expectancy—
The intended meaning is that *samāptapunarātta* (the resumption of what has been concluded) consists precisely in the re-introduction of the word expressing the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

Therefore, the defect of *samāptapunarātta* occurs only in cases where another qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is connected [to the substantive] through an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) raised by questions such as "Of what kind is it? and so forth.

The phrase "acūḍāmaṇi" means that the meaning is obtained from the aforementioned sentence through the word "acūḍāmaṇi," which is formed by the suffix *cvi* prescribed by the rule "the suffix *cvi* occurs when there is the becoming of what was not previously so.
(1) Regarding "for the attention of the disciples": this refers to the attentive focus (*avadhāna*) of the disciples.
The meaning is that there must be a desire to hear from him. For if the subject matter to be explained is not specifically known,
and if the students do not grasp that understanding it is a means to their welfare (*aṣṭasādhana*), the desire to hear the discourse cannot arise,
even when they know through the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) that the author intends to provide a commentary on his own *Kārikāvalī*.

The sense is that, since the nature of the six means of valid knowledge—which consists in the knowledge of the meaning of the *Kārikāvalī*—is easily grasped from the author’s own words, there indeed arises a desire to hear them. Regarding the phrase "conciseness of words":
conciseness is of two kinds, namely, conciseness of words and conciseness of meaning; and among these, by means of the conciseness of meaning, the [utility] of the work...
Anticipating the objection that if it were not expressive of all meanings, it would fail to produce understanding in the uninitiated,

it has been demonstrated here that the term "concise" (saṃkṣepa) refers merely to the brevity of the words in this context; such is the purpose of the word "atisaṃkṣipta" (extremely concise) in the verse.
Manifesting [this], he says "nanu" and so forth. "Svotprekṣā" means having its root in one's own imagination. By this restrictive particle [“eva”]. (2) Rāmarudrī:
"Sat" is of the nature of a genus (*jāti*); that is, it is merely a universal (*sāmānya*), a recurring property (*anugata-dharma*), and in some cases it takes the form of an adjunct (*upādhi*).

In some cases, it is the form of the universal (*jātirūpa*). The sense is that, since the form of the universal itself is what must be defined in the present treatise, the term "commonality of existence" (*satsāmānya*) was stated in order to obtain the form of the universal. Now, one might object: since the word "existent" (*sat*) has the meaning of being qualified by existence (*sattā*), how can the word "existent" have the meaning of the form of a universal?

It must indeed be stated by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, even the word "universal" (*sāmānya*) is well-known among the authors of the treatises as referring specifically to the universal in the form of a genus (*jāti*), according to their technical convention (*paribhāṣā*); otherwise, [the following would occur].

Since the author of the root-text (Mūlakāra) would be guilty of an omission by not stating a qualifying attribute that excludes a "universal" distinct from "genus" in the statement "the universal is accompanied by a particular," and since the term "existent" (sat) would otherwise be redundant, he says: "Or rather... (yadvā). ||3||
"Vipadam means 'that which leads to misfortune'. This [statement] is made with the intention that prefixes (upasarga) possess denotative power (vācakatva);

otherwise, according to the view that they are merely indicative (dyotaka), since they would not denote any meaning whatsoever, it would be impossible for prefixes to possess the status of a word (pada) defined as having expressive power (śakti), and thus the term "vipadam" would be entirely inconsistent. Therefore...

Even in the case of concentration [of meaning], according to the maxim that words denoting a qualified entity, when in proximity to separate words denoting qualifiers, have as their purport the qualificand alone, it is also consistent to demonstrate that the word *ghāta* (striking), when in proximity to the word *vi-* (non-), has as its purport mere absence. Otherwise, for the word *vi-*...

It should be noted that because it would be impossible for the word to denote a qualifier if it did not denote some object at all, the term *vighāta* would not fall within the scope of the aforementioned principle;
this applies even to a word that denotes a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*).

Since the status of being a "denoter of a qualifier"—defined as the capacity to convey a qualifier—remains intact [for these words], it would follow that they could never denote a qualified object; therefore, the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) is used.
This means: distinct from words that denote a qualified object. Now, [one might ask]: was this not composed for the destruction of obstacles?

By the root text stating "maṅgalam" (auspiciousness), it is indicated that auspiciousness is indeed the producer of the destruction of obstacles; therefore, although the doubt raised by the subsequent root text beginning with "nanu" (now, however)— that auspiciousness is not the cause for the destruction of obstacles— is indeed appropriate, nevertheless [it is not so] with respect to completion (*samāpti*).
The statement that "it is the cause" is inconsistent; therefore, he introduces that passage with a different underlying intention, beginning with: "But [is it not so] because of its fruitlessness?
(Rāmarudrī).
Regarding the phrase "by the reason of being devoid of specific fruits": although even in rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma there is a lack of specific fruits in the form of sons and so forth,
and thus the absence of specific fruits is not pervaded by fruitlessness (*niṣphalatva*), nevertheless, by that term [the author] intends the absence of *all* specific fruits whatsoever.

The point is that because [the absence of all specific instances] is intended to be expressed, and because the absence of all specific instances is pervaded by the absence of the general property, there is no inconsistency in what was stated. Nor, for the sake of establishing fruitlessness, should one merely prove the absence of all specific fruits; rather, in the root [text], it is...

By the statement that "auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not the cause for either the destruction of obstacles or for completion," it is established solely that [auspiciousness] is devoid of these two results; however, since this does not establish the reason in the form of being devoid of *all* specific results, how is this relevant to the subject at hand?

This must be stated: since it is universally agreed that auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) are devoid of fruits such as cattle or sons, they are unfit to be established [as causes]; for both the ancient and the modern [schools] accept that the fruits [of auspicious rites] are exclusively the completion [of a work] and the destruction of obstacles.
Therefore, in establishing their being devoid of those two fruits...
The sense is that it is necessary to establish the reason consisting in the emptiness of any specific fruit [for the rite].
Nor is it the case that, even so, because the ancients accepted that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is a cause for completion only by way of the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*),
[auspiciousness] would not be a cause for completion either if it were not a cause for the destruction of obstacles.
It should not be argued that since causality by way of the destruction of obstacles is impossible to assert,

the denial of the separate status of the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) as a cause of completion is entirely redundant; for it is because the ancients have everywhere maintained that the auspicious rite is a cause of completion precisely through the mediation of the destruction of obstacles.

In the view of the modern proponent who maintains that the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*) is the fruit of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) by accepting [the rite] as a cause, the ancient masters argue that there is no such consequence of futility for an auspicious rite performed by one who lacks the absolute absence of obstacles— such as those who possess an inherently established freedom from obstacles.

It is impossible [to establish this], because even in our own view, since there is no such mediating factor as the destruction of obstacles therein, one must simply accept that auspicious rites (maṅgala) are fruitless; thus, there is no fault whatsoever, as the ancients agree that auspicious rites are the cause of completion only through the mediation of an unseen potency (apūrva).

This is the state of affairs. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement of the ancients that "the destruction of obstacles is the medium (*dvāra*) for auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*). For "being a medium" consists in being produced by that [cause] while simultaneously producing what is produced by that [cause]; and this [definition] holds even when auspiciousness is a cause of completion through the medium of the unseen merit (*apūrva*).

Since the destruction of obstacles functions as the cause for the completion produced by auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) by way of being the absence of a relationship with an impediment, and since this destruction of obstacles can indeed be produced by auspicious rites, [the efficacy of] *maṅgala* occurs through the medium of a transcendental potency (*apūrva*).

Even though the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*) is the cause of completion, it is possible for it to serve as an intermediary (*dvāratā*). [Rāmarudrī: Even so, according to the view that the unseen potency (*apūrva*) serves as the intermediary, it must be stated that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is a cause by way of the relation of being connected with the *apūrva* produced by itself; [it cannot be stated] by way of the relation of possessing the destruction of obstacles produced by itself.

It should not be said that the demonstration of causality by the authors of the *Muktāvalī* commentary is entirely inconsistent; for in those infinite instances where the destruction of obstacles produced by auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) exists, there would be the burden of postulating numerous distinct *apūrva* entities. Therefore, in such cases...

The statement is consistent because it intends to show that it is logical for auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) to be the cause of completion (*samāpti*) precisely through the relation of possessing the destruction of obstacles produced by itself. Nor does this imply that, even so,
auspiciousness is the cause of completion in some cases through the relation of the destruction of obstacles produced by itself.
In some cases, it follows that [the cause of completion] is through its connection with an apūrva produced by itself; and thus,

although it is necessary to deny that [the subsidiary acts] are causes of a separate completion, where the auspicious rite (maṅgala) is connected to an apūrva produced by itself, it is not there [connected] to the destruction of obstacles (vighnadhvaṃsa) produced by itself.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that because auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) lacks a positive concomitance with completion through either of two relations— namely, the relation of the destruction of obstacles produced by itself, or the relation of an unseen potency (*apūrva*) produced by itself— the very status of being a cause for completion is impossible to maintain.

The core point is that, by virtue of that relationship, the state of being immediately preceded by an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) is also included within the defining characteristic of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), and thus there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Now, [one might object]: by means of the reason consisting of negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), the absence of causality in completion (*samāpti*) [is established].

Regarding the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), the inference by the proponent (*siddhāntin*)— that the rite is a cause of completion, based on the reason that it possesses fruitfulness while having neither the nature of a means (*sādhana*) nor resulting in any other fruit— is inconsistent, provided that the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) has not pointed out a fallacy in the reason that establishes the absence of its being a cause of completion.

Because the inference [of the cause of completion] would result in being counterbalanced (*satpratipakṣatva*), he states the intended meaning of the Siddhānta text: "of the doubt regarding deviation" (*vyabhicārasaṃdehasya*).

This means: of the doubt regarding the fact that the property of being an auspicious rite (*maṅgalatva*) is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence residing in that which possesses completion.

Regarding the phrase "in the form of a doubt concerning the object of apprehension": for the object to be apprehended by inference is the status of being a cause of completion [of a work] in the case of an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).

And that [status] consists in possessing the nature of an auspicious rite (*maṅgalatva*) which is not a delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence residing in that which possesses completion.
Thus, since a doubt regarding deviation—which culminates in a doubt regarding the probandum—is absent from the inference, [the inference remains valid].

The sense is that it is an obstructive factor (*pratibandhakatva*). Obstructiveness consists precisely in the perception of the causal conditions. This was stated according to the intention of the view that a doubt regarding those [conditions], qualified by the absence of the perception of specific features, is an obstructive factor for perceptual certainty; however, in reality, it is the causal complex of the doubt itself [that constitutes the obstruction].

[The definition is] "the state of being an obstacle to certainty. For this very reason, it should be understood that in the state where a specific feature (viśeṣa) is perceived, there is certainty because the causal complex for doubt is absent due to the obstruction of the manifestation of only one alternative (koṭi). Regarding the phrase "of that in that":
the meaning is "of the doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya) in the case of inference. [Regarding the term] "because of being favorable": [End of excerpt]
The intended meaning is that [the reason] serves to establish *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject) by means of the absence of proof (*siddhyabhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of a reductio ad absurdum (*pariśeṣānumāna*)," the reason consisting in the possession of generality (*sāmānyavattva*), while being characterized by the absence of other specific properties (*taditaraviśeṣābhāvavattva*), constitutes a reductio ad absurdum inference. And as for the phrase "and conduct (*ācāra*) in this case": [it refers to the following].

Here, the word "iti" connects with what follows; thus, although conduct (*ācāra*) is indeed an action, the meaning is that here, because it is heard as the object (*viṣaya*), it is intended to be the completed act (*kṛta*). [Objection:
But surely, since even the Śyena sacrifice is a means to the desired end consisting of the killing of an enemy, its possession of a fruit (*saphalatva*) remains unimpaired; therefore, in that case—

To dispel the objection that even if the reason (*hetu*) exists, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and thus the qualification "uncontested" (*avigītatva*) in the reason is redundant, he says "by that," etc., demonstrating the deviation in the absence of the word "uncontested": "useful for engagement" (*pravṛttyupayuktā*).

For the successful completion of the undertaking of an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), that which is to be inferred as "fruitfulness"— consisting in being a means to a desired end that is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence—

is simply absent in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice; thus, in the absence of the term "uncontested" (*avigīta*) in the reason (*hetu*), there is indeed a logical fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the "forcefulness" (balavatva) of an undesirable [consequence] consists in its being distinct from that which is inseparable from the production of the desired object. Because of this qualification of "forcefulness" regarding the undesirable, there is no lack of motivation toward sacrifices and the like that must be accomplished through great wealth, expenditure, and effort. Even though...

Since even acts such as splashing water on a tree are prohibited by such injunctions as "one should not perform fruitless action," the volition conducive to them also produces a powerful undesirable result in the form of hell; therefore, the subject matter of undisputed traditional practice pertains only to fruitful actions.

The word "śiṣṭa" (refined/learned) is redundant; nevertheless, its purposefulness lies precisely in excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of futile efforts (*vṛthāceṣṭā*) performed by animals and the like.

Since injunctions and prohibitions pertain to human agents, such futile efforts are not the objects of prohibition. *Note: The term *rāmarudrī* appears to be a marginal note or a reference to a commentary.*

The meaning is: "because it does not produce a powerful undesirable result. [The opponent asks: "But then what? This means: "if it is improper to assume an unseen result (adṛṣṭa-phala). [The author replies: "By the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice" (*viśvajin-nyāya*).
In the section on optional rites (*kāmya-prakaraṇa*), the injunction is heard: "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit."

Since it is recited within the section on optional rites (*kāmya-prakaraṇa*), it lacks the character of a compulsory rite (*nitya*); furthermore, because there is no mention of a fruit in the scripture, one must postulate some result for the sake of motivating its performance, as there is no fruit mentioned in the *śruti*. Thus, that [result] is heaven (*svarga*).

Jaimini has composed the aphorism: "Because it is non-distinct with respect to all. That heaven which is to be accomplished by the Viśvajit sacrifice must be [the result], because heaven is non-distinct with respect to all; that is to say, because it is an object of desire for everyone. And thus:
The meaning is as follows: if the Viśvajit sacrifice were to have results such as a son, those who do not desire a son or similar things would not engage in it;
however, if its result were heaven, since that is an object of desire for everyone, the engagement of all people in it becomes possible.
Therefore, heaven alone should be postulated as the result.

In response to the inquiry—"By the phrase 'because it is present' (*upasthitatvāt*), what is meant by its being present?"—he says: "of one who is engaged in a reductio ad absurdum (*pariśeṣānumāna*). Its meaning is: "an inference whose cause is the state of having a result, given that [other] results have been exhausted. [Objection: But surely, the presence of completion (*samāpti*) merely as the property of being completed is of no consequence.
Since there is no difference in the fact that even the absence (abhāva) and other factors constitutive of pervasion (vyāpti) are equally present [in consciousness], he says:

"by virtue of being the object of the desire of a person engaged at the beginning of the treatise. Thus, it is the state of being an object of a presentation (upasthiti) qualified by the mode (prakāra) of being the object of such a desire.

The meaning is that this does not apply to others. It should be understood that such a state [of desire] exists because desire is universal at the time of commencing a work and at the very moment of its completion.
He removes the fallacy of deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). Although, when there is certainty regarding a deviation in the negative concomitance...
Since the status of [the absence of obstacles] as a cause has been refuted, the conclusion that completion is the effect of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not established;
therefore, the inference of auspiciousness from the effect in the form of completion is not possible.
However, if there is doubt regarding auspiciousness performed in another birth...

If it is argued that even the certainty regarding the deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) is merely a doubt, and that this doubt does not act as an obstacle to the inference of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) as a cause— thereby making the inference of auspiciousness possible through completion (*samāpti*)— then:

Since a doubt regarding such deviation— which culminates in a doubt regarding the object of apprehension— is ineffective, the attempt to eliminate such deviation is indeed futile. Nevertheless, even in the case of the inference of causality,
for an atheist there remains a doubt concerning auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) performed in a previous birth.
The sense is that doubt regarding invalidity arises from the doubt that the object [of the cognition] has been sublated;

and since a certainty of causality that is overwhelmed by doubt regarding invalidity is incapable of producing its own effect, it is necessary to eliminate that [doubt]. This is so because of the deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*).

He dispels the objection—"Since completion is itself an effect, how can there be an inference of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) from the effect that is completion?"—with the words beginning "grāhyasaṃdeha" (doubt regarding the object to be grasped). [The opponent objects:
"But in cases where obstacles are numerous, since the destruction of some obstacle is necessarily brought about by some auspicious rite..."

He dispels the objection— "How can there be an absence of completion in this view, given that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) exists through its relation to the destruction of obstacles produced by itself?"— with the words "And thus" (*tathāca*), etc.
[The phrase] "having a number equal to the obstacles" (*vighnasamasaṃkhyāka*) refers to that which resides in all obstacles, excluding those obstacles belonging to that particular instance.

The meaning is: by virtue of being an auspicious act possessing that number, where "that number" refers to a number residing in that locus which is not occupied by any other auspicious acts belonging to the same class as it; otherwise, even when obstacles are abundant...

This is because it is possible to establish an equality of number either by taking the count of whatever obstacles have occurred, even if there is a deficiency in auspicious acts, or by taking the count of whatever auspicious acts have occurred; [the phrase] "from an auspicious act of a greater number" is merely superficial. (Rāmarudrī)
If auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) were the cause by virtue of being a number that possesses a repetition of a type of number established as removing obstacles,

then it would be possible for a greater number of auspicious acts to destroy fewer obstacles. In reality, however, the absence of all obstacles also functions as a cause by way of being the absence of the connection with an impediment (*pratibandhaka*).

The purport of the root text is precisely this: although there is an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) by virtue of its being a cause for completion through its connection with the destruction of obstacles, there is no positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) because the absence of all obstructions— which is included among all the other causes [of the work]— is simply not present [in that case].

It is indeed improper to describe [the number of obstacles] as a cause by virtue of their being equal in number. However, it should be understood that the author of the root text (mūla) takes recourse to the second alternative precisely with the intention that postulating a distinctness (*vaijātya*) characterized by greater strength would be burdened by the fault of complexity (*gaurava*). Nor [should one object] regarding the phrase "an obstacle produced by its own cause" (*svajanakavighna*); here...

Because auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is a cause of completion (*samāpti*) by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*) of the destruction of obstacles (*vighna-dhvaṃsa*) produced by itself;
and because auspiciousness is a cause of completion by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor of the destruction of obstacles produced by itself.

Through the positive concomitance (anvaya) expressed as "because auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the cause of completion by means of the relation of being the locus [of the action], [the latter] being related to the agent's volition (*kṛti*) conducive to the final phoneme of its own counter-correlate," three types of causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) are obtained. Among these, the first two [relations] are based on proximity residing in the body (*śarīraniṣṭhapratyāsatti*).

The third [relation], however, is based on the proximity residing in the self (*ātmaniṣṭha*); it serves as the delimiting relation for causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) in the first alternative and as the delimiting relation for effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) in the second alternative.
Since it is merely a case of simple delimitation (*kevalāvacchedakatā*), the author of the treatise did not mention it because it is easily understood.
This is the point to be understood: by this,

the objection raised by some— that it is improper for the authors of the manual to adopt such excessively cumbersome relations as the delimitors of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) and the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) due to a lack of purpose— is refuted.

[The cause] has no other occasion [for occurrence]. For this very reason, even the following statement is meaningful: otherwise, since completion would arise even in the body of one who dies while performing it—by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor of the destruction of an obstacle to its own producer—even in the absence of an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) in that case, [the aforementioned relation would still hold].

It should be noted that because there is no possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra) given the existence of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) through the relation of being the delimitor (*avacchedakatā*) of the destruction of obstacles produced by itself, it would follow that the inclusion of that [relation] is redundant. As for the phrase "completion in another birth": this is not to be accepted as the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are never observed to practice [the rite] with such an intention; this is the sense.
In this regard, the following should be noted:
since the performance of an auspicious invocation does not require great expenditure or effort, it can be performed even at the time of beginning a work;
furthermore, there is the possibility of omitting it in a future birth when one lacks the capacity for authorship.

This [consequence] does not arise; for no one, out of the expectation of future sovereignty, acquires a white parasol—which can be accomplished with very little wealth—as a matter of necessity. When the capacity to compose a work exists, the undertaking of composing that work is necessary for one who performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) with the aim of completing the work, and it is indeed necessary.

Regarding the phrase "its completion": even if completion does not occur at some point due to an abundance of obstacles and the like, nevertheless, the completion of a future life is not the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) there; for it is possible that, through delusion, only the completion of this life is intended. Therefore:

Regarding the phrase "its own counter-positive": one might object that it should simply be stated that completion [of the composition] is the cause with respect to the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*), rather than pursuing the extension up to the delimitation of the final phoneme which is its own counter-positive. To this we reply: consider a case where, in the second moment following the production of a phoneme, a separation of the body from this location occurs due to a movement of the body.

And by that [separation], there is the destruction of the prior conjunction; however, in that case, there is no destruction of the color (varṇa) with respect to the delimitation of that body, but rather only with respect to the delimitation of the light (prabhā) and so forth residing in the substratum of the body.
Thus, it is not accepted that the status of being a delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) constitutes the relation that delimits the effect-ness (kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandha).

Regarding the phrase "belonging to the same class as that which delimits its own production": there is no rule that completion must occur in the very same body that delimited the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), because at the time of completion, the body that delimited the auspicious rite may have perished due to the accumulation of bodily parts and so forth. Therefore, one must pursue the definition up to the level of "belonging to the same class."

The *jātis* (universals) must be qualified by the property of not residing in two entities that exist at the same moment; therefore, there is no fault even if the body of another birth is of the same *jāti* as the body delimited by the *maṅgala*, due to its being of the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*), and so forth. And such...

Since "birth" (*jāti*) is simply the universal (*jāti*) such as Caitra-ness that resides in every single body belonging to that person during that particular birth, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. Even if one were to state "belonging to the same class as its own delimitant" (*svāvacchedakajātīyatā*), there would still be no fault.

Thus, although the entry into the origin [of the treatise] would otherwise be useless, the entry into the origin is nevertheless included here for the purpose of securing that the destruction of obstacles is also a cause by means of this very same connection; for if auspiciousness is a cause by means of this connection, then the destruction of obstacles is likewise a cause by means of this very same connection.

The phrase "being a cause" (*hetutvam*) refers to the possibility of [the work] being accomplished. However, it must be understood that for the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*) to function as the delimiting relation (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) of the cause, the entry of origination (*utpatti*) is necessary; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that even the completion [of a work] in another birth could be the fruit of the destruction of obstacles. Alternatively, [this may refer to] the auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) consisting of praise.

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, because [the self] is eternal, it is not possible for the body to be its delimiting factor (avacchedaka); rather, it is only the manifestation (prākaṭya) that arises from it which serves as such.
Therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "up to its arising" is solely for the purpose of encompassing the Mīmāṃsaka position.

Regarding the phrase "putrakāmādhikaraṇe": this means the contradiction with the discussion concerning the term *putrakāma* (one desiring a son) in the injunction, "One desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi. Regarding the phrase "svāvacchedakāvacchinna": this refers to where [the two] are simultaneously [present] by both the theist (*āstika*) and the atheist (*nāstika*).

The completion of the work was achieved there; even in the case of the completion of an atheist's work, since it arises at a moment immediately following the destruction of obstacles produced by the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) of a theist, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—namely, the presence of the effect (completion) in its locus prior to that [auspicious rite] through the aforementioned relation—because of the absence of the auspicious rite. Therefore...

The inclusion of "having a counter-positive delimited by its own delimitant" is for the purpose of [defining non-existence]. The introduction of the second relation is to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the end of a nihilist's [existence]. "Posteriority to itself" (*svottaratva*) consists precisely in being the locus of the destruction of the moment that is the locus of itself. And "arising in such a moment" is...

Since the completion [of the rite] by an atheist is indeed common [to both cases], the completion by an atheist must be excluded by means of the very insertion of "immediate succession" (*avyavadhāna*). And that immediate succession consists in the state of not being the locus of the destruction of the second moment— which is the locus of the destruction of the moment that is the locus of the production of the destruction of the obstacle which is its own substratum.

Because it is impossible for [the state of being a non-moment] to exist anywhere at the moment of completion or origination. And if it is said that this [state] consists in not being the locus of the destruction of the moment that is the locus of its own destruction, even then, since the destruction of a destruction is unestablished, such a thing qualified by destruction through those two relations is simply unestablished. As for that which...
Non-interruption (*avyavahitatva*) consists precisely in not being the locus of the destruction of the moment that is the locus of the destruction of its own substratum.

And this is easily established in all cases by taking, through the term "that moment" (*tatkṣaṇa*), the specific instance of the moment immediately preceding completion within the moment of completion; as for the avoidance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the body of a nihilist (*nāstika*):
The claim made by some— that [the definition of non-obstruction] is satisfied by the mere condition of having a counter-positive delimited by its own delimitor—
is utterly false; for, since the destruction of obstacles produced in the self has no further destruction,
that [destruction] would persist in that very self even with respect to the body of another birth which serves as the locus for its experience.
Because the existence of *sattva* (being) is necessary, it is impossible to prevent the occurrence of nihilism (*nāstika*) at the very first moment;

otherwise, since merit, demerit, and so forth acquired in other births would also result in non-existence when delimited by the body of another birth, they could not produce experience within that [body].

It would not be so. Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned defect does not arise because the phrase "its own delimitant" (svāvacchedaka) means its own delimitant of origination; for if that were the case, [the same problem would apply] even to the completion of an Āstika rite.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence of non-inclusion [of certain cases] due to the absence of having as its counter-positive that which is delimited by the very delimiter of its own origination.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault at all because the intended meaning is simply "having as its counter-positive that which is delimited by something belonging to the same class as the delimiter of its own origination," for even so—

If it is argued that, since there is no purpose in defining "non-intervention" (*avyavadhāna*) as mere non-separation, such a definition is difficult to maintain as being redundant—this is true; however, in the present context, "non-intervention" simply means not being subsequent to one's own immediately preceding birth. Furthermore, "birth" is the first conjunction of the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and "primacy" (*ādyatva*) with respect to the body is [defined as follows]:
The definition is: "not being the locus of the destruction of a body belonging to its own class. And the *jāti* (universal) to be understood here is precisely that which was mentioned previously;
thus, there is no lack of establishment (*aprasiddhi*).

Furthermore, since the completion of a non-believer (*nāstika*) occurs at a moment subsequent to the birth following the destruction of obstacles, the exclusion of such cases by including the condition of "immediacy" (*avyavadhāna*) is entirely unassailable.
Nor should it be argued that even the conclusion of the Āstika [period] cannot be included because it arises at a moment subsequent to the birth of another person who follows oneself.

Because birth (*janman*) is to be qualified by being characterized by the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*), through a relation of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) composed of both [the destruction of obstacles] and the state of being the locus of enjoyment delimited by the body which is its own substratum (*svāśrayaśarīra*). Nor does this fail to include such a completion [of a work] after which the author attains liberation; for even in that case, the aforementioned qualification is present.
It should not be argued that [the definition fails] because a birth that is not co-located with its own subsequent [body] is unestablished;
for one must accept that the meaning of the term "immediate" (*avyavadhāna*) is precisely "not being preceded by one's own final body.
Furthermore, "finality" (*caramatva*) consists in not being the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a body belonging to the same class as oneself. And thus:

There is no failure to include [the case] where, even at the place of liberation (mukti-sthala) following completion, there is the manifestation of one's own subsequent final body; and the inclusion of the term "subsequent" (uttara-tva) is for the purpose of excluding those cases where an atheist has completed another work without performing an auspicious invocation (maṅgalācaraṇa), and subsequently—

Having become an *āstika* by means of that very body, he destroyed the obstacle that arose immediately thereafter through auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) and completed the other work; this was done precisely to prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the previous completion [of the first work]. This is the general direction [of the argument]. [This applies] when the cause is not delimited by the nature of the effect.
He states the consensus of the Easterners (Prācām) with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

Even if one accepts that the cause enters into the scope of the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), it is necessary to explain that in the expression "liberation [results] from death in Kāśī," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) signifies the sense of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*); and thus:

With the intention that the ancients do not agree with the view that the cause is not delimited by the nature of the effect, he raises an objection: "Now [atha]... Even if it were possible for the cause to enter into the category of the delimiting condition of the effect, there would still be no possibility of auspiciousness being the cause of completion.

He offers a resolution with the intention that [the relation] is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhatva*): "Even so... [The phrase] "because the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*) must necessarily be an effect" means that, according to the view of the ancients, one would have to postulate both the attainment of completion (*samāpti*) and the destruction of obstacles as effects of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), which constitutes the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). [The text continues: "May obstacles not [hinder] me..."
"Let it cease"—this is the intended desire. This indication [in the text] is restrictive;

otherwise, since the completion [of a work] has its fruit in auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) precisely by way of the destruction of obstacles, there would also be a desire for the destruction of obstacles dependent upon the desire for completion.

Otherwise, because the performance of an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) would result in being irrelevant to the subject at hand by virtue of its being merely a subordinate factor for another [primary] auspicious invocation, or— if one objects: even if both are effects of an auspicious invocation and thus involve complexity (*gaurava*), why is it that only the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*) is the fruit of the auspicious invocation, since it is performed with the desire for the destruction of obstacles?— [the author replies:]...

He dispels the doubt that [auspiciousness] cannot arise from the non-performance of auspicious rites— since there is a rule that one must perform whatever action has a specific fruit out of a desire for that fruit— by stating, "May my obstacles be removed," and so forth. Now, it might be argued that the destruction of obstacles alone is the fruit of auspicious rites.

Anticipating the objection that the statement of the original author is incorrect—on the grounds that since the word "fruit" (*phala*) denotes something produced, the destruction of an auspicious rite (*maṅgaladhvaṃsa*) is also produced by that rite, and thus the use of the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) would be inconsistent—he explains the word "fruit" while refuting that doubt: "The fruit... [and] "accidental... (*ākasmika*).

The meaning is: "not being regulated by any cause whatsoever. Now, one might raise the objection: "In that case, rain would not be the fruit of the Kārīrī sacrifice either, because once the drought has ceased due to the sacrifice, rain occurs from its own [natural] causes. He dispels this doubt by accepting the consequence with the words: "By this very [reasoning]."

*Avagraha* is a specific type of obstacle that prevents rain. [From] Rāmarudrī: [The phrase] "the Veda's capacity to convey causality" means that, according to some, the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is verbal productive energy (*śābdībhāvanā*), according to others it is the *apūrva*, while in the Nyāya school it is the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Thus, regarding the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)...

Since the causality of the destruction of obstacles is sublated [in the case of a failed rite], there would result the invalidity of the Vedic injunction inferred from the conduct of the learned— namely, "one desiring the destruction of obstacles should perform auspicious rites"—
because, according to the Nyāya school, it is precisely that causality of the destruction of obstacles which is established by the injunction regarding auspicious rites.

The intended meaning is that [the performance of auspicious rites] must be accepted as necessary. Now, one might object: "If there is an obstacle, it is the destruction of that very obstacle which is taught by the Veda; therefore, the root text is inconsistent. For just as in the case of "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," so too in the case of "One desiring the destruction of obstacles should perform auspicious rites" and the like, [the destruction of the obstacle would be the result].

The meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) to be expressed is precisely its being the cause for the destruction of obstacles, and not "when an obstacle exists," because there is no word in the text that conveys that latter sense; therefore, he states its underlying purport as follows: "And thus...
In the root text, the phrase "when an obstacle exists" is to be supplemented by "due to auspicious rites" (*maṅgalāt*). And thus...
Even though a jar is not produced when there is only a staff, the statement "the staff is the cause of the jar" does not lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*),
because it is never the intended meaning (*tātparya*) that the staff must always precede the jar immediately. Rather,
[its meaning is] that while all other causes of the jar are present, it is precisely the staff that immediately precedes the jar.

The underlying intention of the root text is that the same applies here as well; this is indicated by the phrase "they attain tranquility," etc., where "etc. includes the statement "by reciting the Gaṇeśa-stava.
Although the fact that the recitation of the hymn is a cause for the destruction of obstacles is indeed conveyed by such statements, [the objection remains].
Since it is impossible for there to be any deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the destruction of obstacles produced by recitation—

given that auspiciousness (maṅgala) in the form of praise exists in the locus of the effect through its relation as being recited by the reciter— the author shows a case of deviation in another instance by stating: "produced by expiatory rites" (prāyaścittajanya).

Revealing the category of *viśeṣa* itself, he says: "And thus" (*tathāca*). He states it for the sake of brevity: "of a different class" (*vijātīya*). [The phrase] "there would be no inclination" (*pravṛtti na syāt*) means that the rule is that only one who desires a particular result will have an inclination toward that which is its cause; such is the intended sense. [The phrase] "inclination must be expressed" (*pravṛtir vācyā*)...

It is like the activity of one desiring satisfaction toward the act of cooking, which is the means for preparing the rice that serves as the means for that satisfaction; this is the remainder [of the argument]. "By way of deviation" (vyabhicāreṇa) means by way of negative deviation (vyatireka-vyabhicāreṇa). "Of the absence of relation as such" (saṃsargābhāvatvena saṃsargābhāvasya) has the final meaning of "of that which is delimited by the property of being an absence of relation" (saṃsargābhāvatvāvacchinnasya).

And it should be understood that this explanation does not eliminate the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even if the absence of conjunction (*saṃsargābhāva*) is a cause by way of being a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and so forth; for the literal reading of the root text does not resolve the aforementioned doubt. Now, if [it is argued that] the various absences of obstacles...
If the causality [of the absence of obstacles] were based on the mere absence of the relation to any obstacle whatsoever, then, given the presence of some obstacle,

there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the completion [of the rite], since the absence of the relation to that obstacle would still exist. If, however, the causality is based on the absence of the relation whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of being an obstacle (vighnatva), then...

Destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) do not possess the status of a cause, because it is not accepted that their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*). And if the causality were based on the collection (*kūṭa*) of absences of relation having obstacles as their counter-correlates, then [this would apply] nowhere at all.

To dispel the objection that completion [of an action] would be impossible—since the simultaneous absence of destruction, prior non-existence, and so forth at a single location is never possible, as they cannot constitute a collective locus (kūṭādhikaraṇatva)—he says: "And here... and "by way of the respective absences of obstacles."

The meaning is: "by way of the absence of a relation whose counter-positive is that specific obstacle. By this, there is no contingency of completion even when an obstacle exists, by taking [the absence of] difference [as the relation]. Nor, even so, is the contingency of completion unavoidable when an obstacle exists.

It should not be argued that this is because even for a specific instance of an obstacle (*vighna*), there exists a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) in the form of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) with respect to duality and so forth;

for it is possible to remedy the aforementioned fault by intending the meaning to be "as a relational non-existence whose counter-positive resides in that specific obstacle, being delimited by a property other than the nature of that specific obstacle (*tat-tad-vighnatva*)."

Even if one accepts that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) also possess counter-positiveness delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), there is still no [solution] even if one formulates the meaning as "by way of being a relational non-existence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the respective nature of an obstacle (*vighnatva*)."

It should be understood as "impairment" (*kṣati*). [The phrase] "possessing the absence of the destruction of obstacles" means "possessing the general absence of the relation with obstacles. Otherwise, according to the literal sense, since even that which possesses the absence of the destruction of obstacles could still possess the absolute absence of obstacles, [the definition would fail] by way of being the absence of the relation with obstacles.
If it were the cause,
then because there would be no possibility of deviation in negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra), the consequence would be that [the reason] is irrelevant; and thus, where...
There is no completion by means of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) alone; for in that case, since there is an absence of the auspicious factor that destroys obstacles, the obstacle itself remains present.

Furthermore, because there is no absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*) whatsoever that has that specific obstacle as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there is a negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) regarding the absence of the relation to that obstacle.

The sense is that [the obstacle] is indeed difficult to ward off. Now, one must necessarily admit that in cases where completion is not observed despite the presence of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), no destruction of obstacles has occurred; otherwise, since the various absences of connection with obstacles would exist [there], [completion would follow].

Since it is impossible to establish the absence of completion [of a work], and since one cannot therefore claim that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) has the destruction of obstacles as its fruit due to the deviation from positive concomitance (*anvayavyabhicāra*), he dispels this doubt with the words "And where... and "Because of the abundance of obstacles. Now, [one might object]: "But..."

Since there is the possibility that completion might still be absent even after an obstacle has arisen immediately following an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), it would be cumbersome to postulate various individual instances of obstacles as well as their causes, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*);
therefore, he says exactly this: "immediately following an auspicious rite."

Regarding the phrase "svapratiyogiprayojakatve" (in being the instigator of its own counter-correlate): the meaning is "by way of the relation of possessing an effort conducive to the final phoneme of its own counter-correlate. Why, then, was it not stated simply as "by way of the relation of being the instigator of itself" in the case of the individual self (*jīvātman*)?

It should not be argued that, although it is impossible for the individual soul (jīvātman) to possess an effort that conforms to itself, it is possible for it to possess the status of being its own instigator (*prayojakatva*), in the form of being the generator of the effort that generates the final phoneme which, in turn, generates itself; for such an instigatory status [is untenable].

The sense is that [the definition] is cumbersome because it involves the inclusion of various causal factors (*nānājanakatā*). He explains the passage beginning with "In some cases" (*kvacit ca*) by means of another method, starting with "In reality" (*vastutas tu*).
Regarding the phrase "the means of completion" (*samāptisādhanam*), if its meaning is taken as "the cause of completion" (*samāptikāraṇam*):

The phrase "in some cases" (kvacit) is incoherent [here]. Since it has been established that the causality [of the absence of obstacles] consists in being the absence of the conjunction with various specific obstacles, all three types of absences are causes in every instance.
This is because the nature of causality is precisely the possession of a property that delimits the status of being a necessary antecedent; therefore, the word "tat" [is used].

He explains: "immediately following the completion. Now, one might object: in a case where the destruction of obstacles (*vighna*) results from an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is incompatible with both antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), absolute non-existence itself would be non-existent;
how then could the destruction of obstacles be otherwise accounted for by it? To this, he says: "destruction, antecedent non-existence," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "as an absence distinct from mutual non-existence": although the absolute absence of obstacles (*vighnātyantābhāva*) exists everywhere, it cannot function as the cause in its capacity as an absolute absence of obstacles, because that [absolute absence]—being composed of eternality—is more cumbersome than the mere absence of the relation with obstacles (*vighnasaṃsargābhāvatva*). And when a simpler property is available, a more cumbersome property [cannot be adopted].

The sense is that since one does not accept [the property] as being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of causality, the causality of all three [factors] follows as a matter of course. "In that respective relation" (*tattatsaṃsargeṇa*) means "in the relation that delimits the state of being an obstructor" (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka-saṃsargeṇa*). "By way of being denotable" (*vācyatvena*)—and thus...

The meaning of the root text "of the absence of the connection with the obstructer" (*pratibandhakasaṃsargābhāvasya*) is that it refers to an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the relation that delimits the state of being an obstructer (*pratibandhakatāvacchedakasaṃsargāvacchinnapratiyogitākābhāva*); this is the intended sense. [The phrase] "due to lack of proof" (*mānābhāvāt*) [refers to the fact that] in a locus of a jar by way of inherence (*samavāya*), [there is no such absence] by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

For it is necessary to establish the distinction between the absence of a jar delimited by the relation of conjunction and the absence of a jar delimited by the relation of inherence, in order to account for the cognitions: "there is no jar by way of conjunction" and "there is no jar by way of inherence in the locus of the jar."

The sense is that while the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of absolute non-existence is accepted as being delimited by a relation, in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), such a [relational] justification is impossible; therefore, its having a counter-positiveness delimited by a relation (*saṃsarga*) is simply unauthentic (*aprāmāṇika*). Now, if the destruction of obstacles were thus not a cause, then the destruction of evil deeds...

Since [the opponent might argue] that there is no contradiction with the subsequent text beginning with "or the absolute non-existence which is established by itself," he explains the term *duritadhvaṃsa* as "the causal complex for the destruction of evil" (*duritadhvaṃsasāmagrī*). This is because, although absolute non-existence is eternal, its relation to the locus is absent during the time when the counter-positive exists; thus, it refers to the absolute non-existence as connected to the locus.

The meaning is that it is being employed as the causal complex for the destruction of obstacles (*duritadhvaṃsa*). He reveals the very reason for preferring the second interpretation with the words "by this" (*etena*). Now, if auspiciousness has the destruction of obstacles as its fruit, why is there an engagement in it with the desire for completion?

It must be established solely as that which produces the destruction of obstacles (vighna) which, in turn, generates completion. Furthermore, since the objection that the destruction of obstacles cannot be said to be the cause of completion due to the presence of counter-examples (vyabhicāra) has already been addressed by the introduction of the passage beginning with "kvacicca" and so forth, this [present argument] is not irrelevant to the subject at hand. Therefore—

He states another objection: "In this way," etc. [Rāmarudrī]: Now, we do not accept that causality consists in the collection (kūṭa) of absences of the contact of obstructions, such that there would be the fault of unestablished existence (aprasiddhi); rather—

Anticipating the objection that this has already been stated as being "by way of the absence of the contact with various obstacles," he states another refutation: "as previously mentioned. Regarding the second explanation, he states the reason for avoiding that fault: "by the aforementioned method. [He then says] "of the absence of the obstructor."
The meaning is: by way of the absence of that specific obstructer, whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the relation that delimits the state of being an obstructer.

Anticipating the objection—"Since there is an obligatory connection between *yat* and *tat*, how can the word *tat* be appropriate in the present verse where the word *yat* is absent?"—he provides the resolution: "The word *tat*," meaning that because the word *tat* here carries its well-known conventional sense, it does not require the word *yat*. [He further explains: "as being the manner of salutation."
The meaning of the word *namaḥ* is an activity conducive to the cognition of one's own inferiority;
the sense is that the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*), which is coreferential with inferiority, is the meaning of the dative case following the word *kṛṣṇa*. [Rāmarudrī:
Since the state of being a limit is of the nature of an ablative relation (*apādānatā*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) alone would express that meaning, and not the fourth case.

Nevertheless, since the status of being an *apādāna* consists precisely in being a limit (*avadhi*) connected with an action, there is no occasion for the application of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) here; rather, the point is that when one intends to express the aforementioned limit of inferiority (*apakarṣa*), the fourth case alone is prescribed by the rule "namaḥ-svasti-... and so forth. And thus:

From the statement "My activity is conducive to the awakening of my own inferiority relative to Śrī Kṛṣṇa," there arises a direct comprehension (*śābdabodha*), because the meaning of the word *namaḥ* is precisely the activity of the utterer. This being the case, [the phrase] "Nārāyaṇam... [is explained as follows].

Even in passages such as "namaskṛtya" and so forth, only the dative case is required after the word *nārāyaṇa*, not the accusative; for since it is impossible for *nārāyaṇa* to be the object of the verb "to do" (*karoti*), the accusative must instead denote the limit of the downward extraction (apakarṣāvadhi) that constitutes the meaning of the word *namaḥ*. This is because the meaning of the word *namaḥ* itself is the object of that [action].

Because it is to be made known, nevertheless, there the meaning of the word *karoti* (he does) is "he brings about [the action] up to the performance of salutation" by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The word *namaḥ* (salutation) serves to indicate the intended meaning; therefore, because of the absence of connection with the word *namaḥ*, the dative case is not used.

[The relation is] of the nature of a qualifier residing in the limit (*avadhi*), which is itself qualified by a qualifier residing in inferiority (*apakarṣa*), which is in turn qualified by an inferiority determined by the cognition of inferiority.

The meaning of the second case (accusative) is precisely "objecthood" (*viṣayatā*). Therefore, it should be understood that in such instances as "Having paid homage to Svayambhū, to Brahmā of immeasurable splendor," the dative alone is used and not the accusative, because one intends to express the meaningfulness of the word *namaḥ*. [This refers to] the delusion regarding the genitive tatpuruṣa compound; [it means] "the state of being the root of all."

The meaning is: "the state of being an inherent cause. The intention is that the conventional designation "seed" is applied only to that which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a tree and so forth.
The meaning is: "the state of being an inherent cause," because the conventional designation "seed" is applied only to that which is the inherent cause of a tree and so forth.

Although the seed is not the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a tree and so forth— since the sprout is produced by its own parts immediately after the destruction of the seed— he says "not indeed," demonstrating that there is a lack of the aforementioned proof regarding God (*īśvara*). [He states] "due to the absence of a mark" (*liṅgābhāvāt*).

The meaning is that there is an absence of a probans (*liṅga*) that establishes an *Īśvara*. It should be noted that comparison (*upamāna*) was not refuted [in this context] because it only establishes the mere capacity (*śakti*). Thus, in the root text, the phrase "likewise the earth, sprouts, and so forth" indicates that the earth, sprouts, and so on constitute the subject (*pakṣa*).

And so, raising the question of what constitutes the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) that is common to the earth, the sprout, and so forth, he says: "But here... [and] "...of the sprout and so forth as well. Thus, if the property of being earth (*kṣititva*) alone is the delimiting condition of the subject, then the sprout too—

The sense is that the separate mention of sprouts and the like as being "earth" (kṣiti) would be purposeless. Now, one might object: "In this context, the word 'kṣiti' does not refer to that which is delimited by the universal *pṛthivītva* (earthness), such that the separate mention of sprouts and the like would be redundant; rather, it refers specifically to the terrestrial globe (*bhūmaṇḍala*)."

And thus, when all things such as the earth, mountains, sprouts, and so forth obtain the status of being the subject (*pakṣa*), one might ask: "What is the property that serves as the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) common to all of them? To this, it is stated that "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) alone is such [a delimitor].
In that case, there would be no point in separately mentioning the sprout and so forth; therefore, he says: "And what is... (*kaś ca...*).

"By way of the delimiting factor" (*avacchedakāvacchedena*). "In that case" means when the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) is the intended goal. Thus, since the establishment of the probandum by way of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not constitute an obstacle to an inference made by way of the delimiting factor, there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*).
The term *bhāvaḥ* refers to the opinion of others; that is, the Cārvāka view. Regarding the phrase *janyapada*:

the sense is that they do not accept eternal earth because it is imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*) to them. Now, [one might object]: in all systems, regarding the qualifiers included within the scope of the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* (the delimiting condition of the subject)...

There is no rule that a purpose must be required; thus, even in the case of eternal earth (*nitya-pṛthivī*), the term "produced" (*janya*) is meaningful solely as a means of excluding sublation (*bādhavāraka*). To this, he says: "of producedness alone.
Now, let it be that producedness alone is the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*); what is lost for us? To this, he says: "and not..."

Regarding the phrase "that too": [it leads to] the consequence of identity. Now, one might ask: what is the fault if there is identity between the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the reason (*hetu*)? It cannot be argued that the fault is simply "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), because at the very time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum with the reason—which serves as the delimiting factor of the subject—is already established.

It must be stated that the apprehension of pervasion—that the reason (*hetu*) is co-locus with the probandum (*sādhya*)—is of a different form from the inferential cognition that "the locus of the reason possesses the probandum" (*hetumān sādhyavān*).

This is because it is only a proof possessing the same cognitive form (*samānākāraka-siddhi*) that acts as an obstacle to inference; [this applies] in the sense of being delimited by the delimitors (*avacchedakāvacchedena*).
Furthermore, if the goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*),
then a cognition that apprehends mere co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not act as an obstacle [to inference].

Although, in an inference where the conclusion is delimited by a specific delimitor (*avacchedakāvacchedena*), there is indeed more than just co-location— namely, the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) of the subject-delimiter (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

[Objection: It might be argued that although it is the same in that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) also appears in the probandum (*sādhya*), and in the cognition of pervasion the state of being the pervader of the reason (*hetu-vyāpakatva*) indeed appears, nevertheless there is a difference because in the apprehension of pervasion it appears as a qualifier (*prakāratā*), whereas in the inference (*anumiti*) it appears as a constituent of the relation belonging to the probandum. [Response: This is not so, because if the delimitant of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) were identical, it would follow that a verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) could not arise from the *upanaya* sentence.
Because of its being a defect; for even according to the view of the moderns— who accept that verbal cognition can have a deeper penetration regarding the element to be enjoined—

the verbal cognition produced by the *upanaya* sentence, which takes the form "the subject (pakṣa) possesses the reason (hetu) that is pervaded by the probandum (sādhya)," [remains valid] despite the identity between the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the reason (*hetu*).

It should not be said that there is no inconsistency; for since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is already obtained from the example statement (*udāharaṇa*) by the ancients, there would be redundancy in its being presented again by the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, in this view, the application must convey merely the fact that the subject possesses the reason (*hetumat*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this is because [the opponent] accepts that the meaning of the *upanaya* statement "and so is this" is simply that the subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the reason (*hetumat*), and thus, according to that very view, there is an identity between the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the reason (*hetu*), which serves as the basis for their objection.

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of an essential relation" (*svarūpasaṃbandharūpa*): although the individual instances of being an effect (*kāryatā*)—which consist in essential relations—are restricted to their respective individual instances and thus do not possess a commonality that could serve as a delimiting factor for the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), the intended meaning is that they function as the delimiting factor for the subject when they are made common through the property of being "any one of them" (*anyatamatva*). Regarding the phrase "being the counter-positive of prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāvapratiyogitva*): nor... [text continues].

It should not be argued that, since counter-positiveness (pratiyogitva) is also of the nature of an essential relation (svarūpasaṃbandha), the identity of the various individual substrates (dharmivyakti) results in the failure to avoid the identity of the property delimiting the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) and the reason (hetu);
for the reality of an entity consists in its being devoid of non-existence.

According to the intention of the Teacher’s view expressed in the passage beginning with "pratiyogitā," the distinction between the absence of a jar through conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the absence of a jar through inherence (*samavāya*) must be established solely on the basis of the difference in counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*),

because there is identity between the counter-correlative and the delimitors of counter-correlativity. Furthermore, regarding counter-correlativity in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*):

Furthermore, since the counter-positive (pratiyogin) and the individual jar are one and the same, their difference would be impossible to establish; therefore, there would be no distinction between the two. Consequently, just like "objectness" (viṣayatva), "counter-positiveness" (pratiyogitva) must also be accepted as a distinct category of meaning (padārthāntaratva). As for the sevenfold division of categories, [it remains as follows:]...

This statement is made according to the view of the moderns (*navīna*), on the grounds that there is no contradiction [with the definition], since it refers only to those objects of knowledge that are useful for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). In reality, however, the text [refers] to the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), as being the cause.
