It should be understood that there is no fault whatsoever, because the intended meaning is that antecedent negation (*prāgabhāva*) functions as a cause by way of the relation of identity known as "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitā*). In reality, however, regarding the root text's statement "earth, sprouts,
and so forth," if the delimitors of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) are earthness, sproutness, or the nature of that particular jar, [the following applies].

Regarding the intended meaning (*tātparya*): in that context, in the first formulation—"the earth has a creator"—if the objective is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as co-extensive with "earth-ness" (*kṣititva-sāmānādhikaraṇyena*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in part, because [the property of having a creator] is already established in relation to jars and the like. However, if the objective is such that it is delimited by the delimitors of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedakāvacchedena*), then [the fallacy applies] in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Therefore, the pursuit of "sprout-ness" (*aṅkurātva*) as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is undertaken;

and since the intended goal there is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is neither partial proof of what is already established (*aṃśataḥ siddhasādhana*) nor sublation (*bādha*), because the absence of being producible by the effort of a living being (*jīvīyakṛtisādhyatvābhāva*) does not exist in any sprout whatsoever.
The meaning is that there is no such thing as an eternal sprout. Now, one might object:

an inference of having an agent (sakartṛkatva) based on the reason of being an effect (kāryatva), whether delimited by the property of being earth (kṣititva) or by the property of being a sprout (aṅkuratva), is not possible, because the reason in the form of "being an effect" is not a probans that necessitates the conclusion (aprayojaka).

Nor should it be argued that there is no lack of probative force because of the existence of a favorable *tarka*— namely, that if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) were to deviate from being produced by an agent (*kṛtijanyatva*), then it could not be the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of being produced by an agent. This is because [the reason] exists as "having been made" (*kṛtatvena*).

Because there is no evidence for a causal relation on the basis of being an effect, the aforementioned reasoning does not apply. Nor should it be argued that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone constitute such evidence; for one grasps positive and negative concomitance specifically in the form: "When the potter's action exists, the jar exists; when [the action] is absent, the jar is absent."

At the time of a weaver’s production [of cloth], in order to prevent the production of a jar, it is necessary that there be a causal relation between being produced by a potter and being a jar, as qualified by those specific properties; for there is no evidence for a causal relation between being produced in general and being an effect in general. Nor is it the case that...
It must be said that there is indeed a restrictive rule regarding the two specific instances;

for even that [rule] lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*). Nor is there any complexity (*gaurava*) in taking the aggregate (*kūṭa*) of absences of the potter’s activity as the cause for the absence of the general effect, rather than a single absence qualified by the property of being an action (*kṛtitva*).

In that case, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). And this parsimony is not possible unless *kṛtitva* (the nature of being an agentive effort) serves as the delimiting property of the instrumentality (*karaṇatāvacchedakatva*), because it is only the absence of a property delimited by the causal determinant (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-dharma*) that can be the motivator for the absence of a property delimited by the effect-determinant (*kāryatāvacchedaka-dharma*). And thus...
It should not be said that the principle "between two particulars," etc., is rooted solely in parsimony (*lāghava*).

There is no rule that only the absence of a property delimited by the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakadharma*) is the determinant (*prayojaka*) for the absence of the effect; rather, the nature of being a determinant—in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*)—is established in accordance with empirical cognition (*pratīti*).
The rule is that [an absence] is postulated as being delimited by a property that is both simple and non-overlapping. And thus, precisely due to parsimony (lāghava),
there exists a single absence whose counter-positive is qualified by "effort-ness" (kṛtitva) as its non-delimiting causal factor.

The state of being the motivator for the absence of an effect (*kāryābhāvaprayojakatva*) is easily established even without a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on the nature of effort (*kṛtitva*) and the nature of an effect (*kāryatva*); it is with this intention that the word "etc. (*ādi*) was employed, so as to include the specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) residing in a jar at the time of the beginning of creation (*sargādyakālīna*). Thus, regarding that particular individual...

The point is that since what is to be proven is "being produced by a potter," and since there exists a causal relation between "the action of a potter" and "being a jar," there is no room for the suspicion of irrelevance (*aprayojakatva*) in this case. Nor should it be argued that this would entail that God is a potter.

For it is precisely one who is capable of making a jar that is intended by [the opponent] as the potter in the case of God; therefore, even scriptural passages such as "Obeisance to the potters and to the smiths" are consistent with this view.
Furthermore, since the jar at the beginning of creation is the subject of dispute, [the argument applies to] a jar existing at the time of the beginning of creation.

If it is thought that there is a lack of establishment of the subject (*pakṣāprasiddhi*) because [the world] has parts, then let a broken jar (*khaṇḍaghaṭa*) itself be the referent of the word "etc."; for we consider it logical that even prior to that, since the activity of the potter exists, the establishment of God is necessary through an inference having that as its subject (*pakṣaka*).
This will become clear further below. [Objection: Surely, "having an agent" (sakartṛkatva) must mean being produced by an agent.

But that is not possible; for if the agent were the cause, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava), as the causal status would have to be delimited by an infinite number of individual acts (kriyāvyakti). Rather, it is simpler [to define it] in terms of its essential nature (svarūpataḥ).

Disposing of the objection that the universal *kṛtitva* (the nature of being an agent) alone serves as the delimiting condition for causality, [the author], after refuting the views of the ancients, begins to define "having an agent" according to his own position—stating: "And the probandum... (*sādhyaṃ ca*).

The Lord (Īśvara) must be established as possessing eternal knowledge, will, and action through the inference of having a creator; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to establish eternal knowledge and will in the Lord. Therefore, "having a creator" consists precisely in being produced by an immediate knowledge, desire to act, and volition directed toward the material cause.

It is to be established as follows: when eternal knowledge, will, and action are proven by inference, then through an inference based on the reason of being a quality (*guṇatva*) with that [eternal triad] as its subject (*pakṣa*), it is established—by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*)—that they reside in a single substance; and that very substance is God. Thus, there is one God who possesses eternal knowledge, will, and action.

"This is established"—this is the intention of the ancients. Regarding the phrase "because of sublation" (*bādhāt*): the meaning is that there is sublation in the case where [the action] is taken as being of the nature of an effect (*kārya*). Now, one might object: since the causality of knowledge and desire is not established due to the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [how can they be causes]? [The answer is: it is by virtue of being an operation (*vyāpāra*) alone that [they are causes] for the action (*kṛti*).
Regarding the principle that "causality is [defined] solely with respect to the effect," the agent (vyāpārin) is not otherwise established by means of the operation (vyāpāra);
because this would contradict the rules of logic (*nyāya*), he states "by way of an example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) so that those two are not otherwise established.
[He adds] "due to impossibility."

The point is that there is an absence of a single, common property delimiting the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) that pervades both the probandum as it occurs in the example and as it occurs in the subject (pakṣa).
Now, one might object: "In that case, the word 'sva' (one's own) must indeed be abandoned;
for if, through positive and negative concomitance, it were established from the very beginning that only *kṛti* (volitional effort) [is the cause] in all effects..."
If it is insisted that causality is determined solely by the capacity to produce [an effect],
and that there is an inference of knowledge and desire [in the creator] based on that alone, then let those two also be considered "established otherwise" (anyathāsiddha);
nevertheless, being produced by an action whose object is the material cause (*upādāna*) remains the very definition of having a creator (*sakartṛkatva*).
Anticipating the objection that "there is no harm for us since [the property] is yet to be proven" (*sādhyatvāt*), he says: "with reference to its being produced" (*kṛtatvāpekṣayā*).
He defines "having an agent" (*sakartṛkatva*) according to his own view with the words: "but rather... (*kiṃtviti*).
He himself explains the purpose of the phrase "delimited by the relation of being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatāsambandhāvaccchinnetyasya*) with the words beginning "by that" (*tenaitayādi*).

He will say: the inclusion of being delimited by "being an effort" (kṛtitva) is for the purpose of ensuring that, when effort is the cause [of action] by virtue of having an object (saviṣayakatva), there is no possibility of knowledge and desire being otherwise established (anyathāsiddha), since those two also function as causes by virtue of having an object; however, by itself...

This is with the intention that one must indeed accept the "otherwise-established" (anyathāsiddhatva) status of those two [the potter's staff and the potter's father]. As for the inclusion of the qualification "being delimited by the relation of inherence" (samavāya-sambandhāvacchinnatva) in the definition of being an effect (*kāryatva*), it is for the purpose of excluding the contingency of a jar arising from its threads and so forth, based on the restrictive rule that "an effect exists in that very locus where the activity directed toward it occurs, and that effect exists there by way of inherence. *Rāmarudrī*: [The inclusion of this qualification] is intended to prevent the undesirable consequence that a jar would arise in its constituent threads, etc., by virtue of the rule: "An effect exists in that very place where the causal activity is directed, and it exists there through the relation of inherence. This is because, without such a restriction, the activity directed toward a jar might occur in the threads, yet the jar would not necessarily inhere in them. By specifying that the effect must be delimited by the relation of inherence, the possibility of a jar inhering in its threads—which do not stand in the relation of material cause (*upādāna*) to it—is ruled out. Thus, the definition of being an effect remains restricted to its proper domain.
It should be understood that this is stated solely for the sake of establishing the conclusion (*nirvāha*). It is not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

The point is that such a generative capacity (*janakatā*) is delimited by its own connection with the produced *dṛṣṭa* (visible result), and therefore it is not delimited by the relation of objective predication (*viṣayatā*). Now, if a permanent volition (*nityakṛti*) is thus established by the aforementioned inference, then in that regard—

Even if the existence of God as an eternal agent is established by the inference that [an effect] must reside in a substance (*dravyāśritatva*), eternal knowledge and eternal will would not thereby be established for Him. Nor can knowledge and will be inferred in God from His activity, on the grounds that knowledge and desire are the causes of activity.

This must be stated: since it is possible to infer a cause through its effect alone, and because an eternal action lacks the nature of an effect, it cannot be established by inference; with this intention, he follows another method to establish knowledge and desire, beginning with "If, however... (yadīti).

In our own view, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is *kṛti* (volitional effort) alone that is the cause of every effect. Through the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whoever acts, knows, and desires"—one postulates knowledge and desire by means of an effort produced [by them], as being the cause of that [effort]; however, this does not apply to eternal effort, because it is unproduced (*ajanya*).

Inference for both knowledge and desire is simply not possible. However, [the author] stated "if, moreover" (yadi ca), intending his own view that the proof of knowledge and desire must be asserted through scripture itself, such as the passage beginning with "He who is omniscient. The phrase "or being produced by an effort" (kṛtijanyatva) is used because there is no decisive evidence (vinigamanāviraha) [to prefer one over the other]. This is the intended meaning.

And thus, the point is that by the inference of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*) alone, the triad of knowledge, desire, and volition is established in God. As for the phrase "because of the lack of evidence" (*mānābhāvāt*): [an objection might be raised] that, indeed, the agent of a sacrifice stands in the relation of being the locus (*viśeṣyatā*) of his own volition (*kṛti*), while [the effect] stands there in the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Since it might be argued that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone are the means of proof for [the definition] "that which is to be produced" (*kārya*), he says: "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*). Now, one might object: "If one attempts to prove that [an effect] has 'being produced by an effort' (*kṛti-janyatva*) as delimited by 'being produced' (*janyatva*) with the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as the delimiting relation, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) and a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum is absent in cases such as destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Anticipating this objection, [he says...]

otherwise, one would have to postulate a single causal relation between "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and "inherence-in-substance-ness" (samavetadravyatva) based solely on the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance through [the specific properties] such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and "staff-ness" (daṇḍatva).

This is because, by way of logical consistency, it would follow that the status of being a cause of jars and the like through [properties such as] "being a staff" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth would be dissolved.

Nor can it be argued that, even if a specific causal efficacy is established through the aforementioned positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the presence of the effect follows from the presence of the effort (*kṛti*), while in the absence of the effort— [the effect is absent]. (Note: The text appears to be fragmentary here.)

It must be stated that the absence of an effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for even in the absence of the nature of being an effect, the causal relation is unavoidable. This is because, at the time of creation, the general absence of volitional effort (*kṛti-sāmānyābhāva*) and the general absence of an effect (*kārya-sāmānyābhāva*) are not observed anywhere, [and likewise] at the time of dissolution.
Furthermore, due to the non-existence of persons such as ourselves, the very apprehension of such positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is unestablished.
There is a general rule that the apprehension of the causal relation between two things delimited by a particular property occurs only between those two things delimited by that same property.

With this intention, he says: "of the postulation of a single cause alone. For in the present case, there exists a subverting factor in the form of the ascertainment of complexity (gaurava) regarding the infinite causal relations delimited by potness, clothness, the agency of the potter, the agency of the weaver, and so forth; therefore, there is only one causal relation between effectness and agency.

The sense is that it is so postulated. Now, one might object: in order to prevent the production of a jar when the activity of a weaver is present, it is necessary—based on specific positive and negative concomitances—to postulate specific causal relations between the effect and its cause, such as "jar-ness" and "the activity of a potter," and so forth.
The postulation of another general causal relation based on the properties of being an effect and being an action, through such apprehensions of positive and negative concomitance, is groundless,
even when assuming a general causal relation.
Because such a prolixity must be accepted, he states another reason to prove that point: "yadviśeṣayoḥ" (of two particulars).
The principle is that when there is a causal relationship between two particulars, provided there is no subverting evidence, it holds for their generalities as well.
In the Mīmāṃsaka view, color is the cause for visual perception, and touch is the cause for tactile perception.

However, neither color nor touch is the cause for the general category of external sensory perception, because there is a deviation in the case of the perception of light and air. Nor is "quality" (guṇa) the cause, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Nor is either form or touch the cause, because each would also be overly complex (*gurutvāt*), and because, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā-viraheṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of two excessively complex causalities; therefore, it was stated that "in the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). And [it is said] "because of its necessity (*āvaśyakatvāt*)," [referring to] the pervader (*vyāpaka*). By the pervaded (*vyāpyena*).

The meaning is: "because of the certainty of pervasion. Regarding "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*): the sense is that the aforementioned principle is not without a basis in valid cognition, because it is rooted in parsimony. Nor [is it the case] that, even though "agency-ness" (*kṛtitva*) is not the delimiting factor for the causality toward that which is delimited by "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*), [the conclusion follows] precisely from parsimony.

It must be stated that a single absence delimited by "having been produced" (*kṛtatva*) is to be postulated as the cause of the general absence of the effect; for the underlying idea is that there is an invariable rule that only the absence of a factor delimited by the property that delimits causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-dharma*) can be the cause of the absence of a factor delimited by the property that delimits effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).

Therefore, with the intention that there is no evidence for such a rule, he introduces the view of some— beginning with "But some..."— with the words "let it not be. [He says this] because, since there is no evidence for the aforementioned rule,
even if one does not accept such a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), [the desired result follows] simply from parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the absence of effort (*kṛtyabhāva*).

The sense is that it is possible for [the absence of the effect] to be the cause of the non-existence of the effect. The phrase "they say" (āhuḥ) indicates a lack of conviction. The reason for this is that since others do not even accept the beginning of creation (sarga), if a pot existing at that time were taken as the subject (pakṣa), [the argument would fail].

The subject itself is unestablished. In reality, however, by taking a broken pot as the subject (*pakṣa*) and proving that it is produced by the creative act of a potter, the existence of God is established because the creative act of a living being (a human potter) is sublated; for [the potter] must be one capable of making a pot.
Since it is possible to accept such potterhood in God as well by virtue of His being a potter,
we consider it logical that the Vedic scripture, "Obeisance to the potters," is likewise consistent; and even the author of the Dīdhiti explains it in this very manner.
He states this very point: "But for the author of the *Dīdhiti*, even the eternal body...

Since the nature of being a body—defined as being a final whole possessing motion—is impossible in the case of eternal things, and since in his own system every composite whole (*avayavin*) is perishable, there is no possibility here of an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
[The opponent says: "Existence [is the cause]. [The author replies: There is no evidence for existence being the cause by way of being an action (*ceṣṭā*).

Now, it might be argued that when another pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*) exists that is more subtle and whose deviation has not been grasped, causality does not belong to the pervader (*vyāpaka*) form because of the fallacy of superfluousness (*anyathāsiddhi*). Otherwise, [causality would be attributed to the pervader] just as the state of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) is [the cause] with respect to a jar delimited by the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*).

Since it would follow that [the body] could also be a cause by virtue of its being a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth, one must necessarily accept causality solely through the property of being an effort (*iṣṭatva*). Because of this underlying unease, he sets forth the view of the followers of the Ācārya, beginning with the words "The Ācārya... and "Because of the acceptance of a specific difference in kind (*vaijātya*). And thus:

The point is this: since the production of various effects such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth is possible solely through the power of the activity (*kriyā*), motion (*ceṣṭā*), and form (*rūpa*) of atoms (*paramāṇu*), there is no proof for a body of the Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from those atoms, in accordance with that [explanation]. [Objection: But surely, since movement is defined precisely as bodily action (*śarīrakriyā*), and since... [in the case of] an atom... *Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary commentary (likely from the *Rāmarudrī*) following the main argument. The translation reflects the logical structure of the philosophical critique.*

Since the state of being a final whole (antyāvayavitva) consists in the absence of the nature of a body that possesses activity, how could it be possible to accept that the motion of an atom is an instance of "volitional effort" (ceṣṭā)? For "final wholeship" is defined as being a whole that does not originate another substance; and this [quality] is not possible in an atom.

Because an atom is the originator of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and lacks the status of being a composite whole (avayavin), [the definition would fail]. However, if the mere possession of motion were the definition of a body, then there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of applying the term "body" even to the hand and so forth; anticipating this objection, he says: "The definition of a body... [is as follows].

The meaning is that the definition of a body is untenable; thus, regarding the conventional usage of "body" with respect to the hand and so forth, there is simply the acceptance of the desired consequence (iṣṭāpatti). Alternatively, in the definition of a body, instead of the property of being a final whole (antyāvayavitva), one should adopt the property of being distinct from a whole that initiates another substance (dravyārambhakāvayavibhinnatva); and in that case, [the definition] does not apply to the hand and so forth.

The consequence of applying the conventional designation "body" to it [the aggregate] follows from its being the originator of a substance in the form of a body. Alternatively, the ultimate truth is that atoms do not incur the impossibility of being bodies because they lack the status of being composite wholes (*avayavin*). Thus, the proof of its distinctness [from the atoms] is established.

The sense is that, just as in the case of various substrata, the postulation of non-existence in each individual substrate would involve complexity (gaurava), whereas the establishment of a single non-existence distinct from those substrata is achieved through parsimony (lāghava), so it is here as well. Regarding the phrase "having an effect that is difficult to account for":
if one were to accept that God possesses a single body in the form of an atom, then [the world] would arise through its movement.

The meaning is that it is impossible for multiple effects located in different places to arise simultaneously, and it is impossible for an action in one location to produce an action in parts situated in another location.
"Establishing inference" (*sthāpanānumāna*) refers to the inference: "That which is produced is produced by an effort (*kṛti*), because it is an effect."

This is the meaning. "Produced" (*janya*) means produced by an effort (*kṛti*). [The term *sthāpanā* is used] because the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), namely "because it is not produced by a body," was previously raised;
therefore, the word *sthāpanā* (establishment) is used to exclude that. Its meaning is: that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) to be established by itself.
"And because it does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*). This is according to his own system;
however, according to the view of those who follow the Teacher (Dharmakīrti), it should be understood that even sprouts and the like are produced from the body of God in the form of atoms.

Regarding the phrase "of having a doubtful limiting condition" (*saṃdigdhopādhitvasya*): for it is only when a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is ascertained that the ascertainment of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason (*hetu*) can occur by means of the reason's being "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*). Furthermore, when there is doubt regarding a limiting condition, doubt regarding deviation is necessarily present, because of the doubt regarding the pervaded (*vyāpya*).

This is because pervasive doubt is established by experience. For the intention is that since the general cognition of deviation is an obstacle to the cognition of pervasion, even a doubtful upādhi (limiting condition) possesses the capacity to invalidate [the inference].
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the doubt regarding deviation is produced by the doubt regarding the upādhi?"

It must be accepted as being included within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself; for since the probandum (*sādhya*) is ascertained in the case of a jar and so forth, doubt regarding the probandum is impossible there. Furthermore, such doubt does not obstruct the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that includes the subject within its scope does not act as an obstacle to that [knowledge].

Otherwise, since a doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) would be possible in every case prior to the inference, and since the reason (*hetu*) is ascertained therein, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of inference; therefore, it is simply the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), which is determinate with respect to the aspect of the absence of the probandum, but common to both doubt and certainty with respect to the aspect of its presence.

It must be accepted as an obstacle. Now, in the present context, since such a doubt regarding deviation is impossible, how can a doubtful upādhi (extraneous condition) be a defect? With this intention, he raises an objection, beginning with "na ca" (but not).

Regarding the phrase "of the subject and its similar instance" (*pakṣatatsamayoḥ*): the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is that which is delimited by the delimitor of the property to be designated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).
Its "similar instance" (*tatsama*), however, means that which, while being different from the subject, is pervaded by doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).

Regarding the phrase "because of being an obstacle": it is not the case that, according to the aforementioned method, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference (*anumāna*).

It should be stated that, because of the favorable *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum)—namely, "If smoke were non-deviant from fire, it would not be produced by fire"—even the doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is impossible; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the point at hand, the author cites the consensus of the great commentators: "For this very reason," etc. [End of] Rāmarudrī on the favorable *tarka*.

Regarding the phrase "by existence" (*satvena*): the sense is that it is precisely the doubt of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) produced by the absence of a favorable *tarka* (reductio) that acts as an obstacle to the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding the phrase "from certainty": the ellipsis is to be supplied with "because a doubt regarding the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is impossible.
Now, if inference alone were the means of proving God...
In order to dispel the doubt that the study of those portions of the Upaniṣads which expound that [Brahman] would be fruitless,

he introduces the citation from the root text beginning with "dyāvābhūmī" (Heaven and Earth), which establishes the authority of the Veda as well, by saying "evam" (Thus) and "yaḥ sarvajñaḥ" (He who is omniscient).

The meaning is that he possesses knowledge of all objects in a general form. Since even individual souls possess knowledge of all objects in a general form, [the text specifies] "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*);
the meaning is that he possesses knowledge of all objects even in their specific forms. *Tapaḥ*.

The meaning is that it is a means for the destruction of sin, like the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and other such rites. "Inference from the effect" (*kāryānumāna*) means an inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is the effect.
Furthermore, in the verse beginning with "the production of the effect" (*kāryotpatti*), the word "effect" (*kārya*) and so forth [is used].

This refers to an inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is that [destruction]. In this context, the inference "the destruction of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is produced by effort" establishes God through the mediation of an inference regarding action (*kṛti*); however, the inference "the usage of objects such as jars is prompted by an independent person," and so forth, establishes God directly.

The distinction is to be understood. "He promises" (pratijānīte) means that the undertaking of one's own duty is the "promise" (pratijñā). This is because, in the verse beginning with "Substance, quality," etc., there is no presentation of one's own duty regarding the definition of substance and so forth; therefore, [the author] "promises."

Thus, because this is inconsistent, he completes the remainder [of the sentence] with the words "they are defined" (*nirūpyante iti*). [The phrase] "a number that is too few or too many" means that the purpose of making the classification is precisely to exclude such cases; this is the intended sense. [The question] "Why is it not defined? [is answered by: "The category of objects (*padārtha*) is twofold: existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*)."

The meaning is: why has it not been defined by the method that "the six categories beginning with substance (dravya) are positive entities (bhāva), while the remainder is negative entity (abhāva)"? Regarding the phrase "of the seventh" in the root text:
although even if the seventh were stated to be a negative entity, it would still be difficult to establish that the others are positive entities.
For when the status of one person as a Brāhmaṇa has been established, it does not follow that the non-Brāhmaṇa status of all others is thereby established;
nevertheless, because this is a statement of classification,
its nature as a classification consists precisely in the description of mutually exclusive, pervading properties (*vayāpyadharma*).
The point is this: if substances and the like were non-existents (*abhāva*), then "non-existence" itself would not serve as a differentiator;
therefore, since substances and the like do not lack the nature of existence (*bhāvatva*), it follows that they possess existence by default.
Regarding the term "inherence" (*samavāya*): although inherence does not [possess existence] through a co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) defined by inherence...

Although existence (sat-tva) resides in its locus solely through the relation of essential identity (svarūpa-sambandha), it should nevertheless be understood that even if "inherence-ness" (samavāyatva) is not the delimiting factor for the relationality [of inherence], there is no loss of the fact that inherence itself resides [in its locus] by means of inherence, because inherence is its own relation by virtue of being an essential identity. This is what is meant by the phrase "attained by implication" (arthāt-prāptim).

The meaning is that [the property] is obtained through inference (*anumāna*). And the inference is of the following form: "Substances and other categories (*bhāva*) possess properties that are non-co-located with the property of non-existence (*abhāvatva*). Nor should it be argued that the non-co-location of the property of non-existence with the class-properties (*vibhājakadharma*) such as substanceness (*dravyatva*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
Since the very nature of "division" consists in the presentation of as many general properties as possible in the form of pervading attributes that do not share a common substratum with one another,
if those [properties] such as *dravyatva* (substance-ness) were to coexist with the general property of *abhāvatva* (non-existence-ness), then...

The meaning is that the very nature of being a cause (*vibhājakatva*) is untenable. Regarding the term "final" (*carama*): finality with respect to the conjunction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body consists in not being the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a breath-conjunction occurring in a body belonging to the same class as itself.
It should be understood that being "primordial" (ādyatva) likewise means not being the locus of the destruction of such a conjunction with breath.

"Metaphorical" (gauṇa) means figurative (lākṣaṇika). "The nature of suffering" (duḥkhatva) is the state of being denotable by the word "suffering. [In the commentary] Rāmarudrī states: "But the relation to suffering is of the nature of being a producer (janakatva), and so forth."

[The opponent says: "But surely, because it is connected with suffering, pleasure cannot possess the nature of suffering, since it is not connected with suffering. Nor should it be argued that the nature of suffering remains intact for pleasure because it is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with suffering; for if that were so, [the same would apply] to the absolute cessation of suffering as well."

Because it would follow that [the final state] is suffering by virtue of its being co-present with the suffering of the past; nor is there [an end to suffering] in the case of the absolute cessation of suffering,
since [that cessation] is not co-present with any suffering in its own locus, whereas [the state in question] is of the nature of being co-present with suffering in its own locus and so forth.

It should not be argued that because the connection with suffering has not been stated in the case of cessation (*nivṛtti*), there is no suffering therein; nor should it be said that in the pleasure of those such as ourselves, that [suffering] is indeed present because it is simultaneous with such suffering. Even so, in the pleasure of heaven, [it is defined] as "that which is not [mixed] with suffering..."

Since it is impossible to accept such a state [of pleasure] because it contradicts scriptural passages such as "intermingled" (*saṃbhinna*), one might suspect that its nature as suffering cannot possibly exist; to dispel this doubt, he says: "of the pleasure of heaven and so forth. Thus, in the scriptural passage beginning with "that which is not mingled with suffering," the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*)— [The remainder of the sentence is: —refers to that which is characterized by the nature of being subject to destruction (*vināśitva*). Therefore, even though the pleasure of heaven and so forth is not inherently suffering, it is designated as such because it is invariably associated with that which is suffering, namely, the nature of being subject to destruction. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the aforementioned scriptural passage. Furthermore, since the pleasure of heaven and so forth is not eternal, it is indeed suffering by virtue of its impermanence, just like the suffering of hell and so forth. Therefore, the statement that "pleasure is not suffering" is intended to show that it is not suffering in the same manner as the suffering of hell and so forth. If one accepts that the qualifier of the qualified (viśeṣṭa) is the motivator by taking recourse to its being the motivator of the portion that is the qualifier, then there would result the undesirable consequence of the linguistic usage: "fire is the motivator of the smoke on the mountain," just as one says, "fire is the motivator of the smoke."

"Of the qualities existing in its own subsequent moments" means: by way of the relation of origination, [the destruction occurs] due to the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) existing in its own subsequent moments.
By this, even though a thing itself exists in its own subsequent moment, there is no consequence of cognition (*jñāna*) and the like being momentary;
nor is there the consequence that the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) would be destroyed by the very conjunction with a jar or other object produced in the second moment.

Since it is impossible for duality and so forth to persist for three moments, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of duality must be said to occur at its own third moment by means of a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) that arose in the second moment after its own production; however, since duality does not exist at that time, the perception of it would be untenable. Nor [is there a solution] regarding the object in the case of direct perception...

It must be stated: even if [duality] is the cause, since duality exists in the second moment, what obstacle prevents its perception from arising in the third moment? [The answer is: because in the case of perception, the object functions as a cause by virtue of existing at the time of the effect; thus, [perception cannot arise] at the moment of destruction.

Because the direct perception of a counter-positive contradicts experience, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the perception of duality in the third moment, provided that dualities and the like persist for three moments. Nor [is there an objection] even if causality is established by the property of being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇatva*). [End of Rāmarudrī].

It should not be argued that the perception of duality would remain impossible because duality would not perish in the third moment when the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) perishes due to the knowledge arising at the moment of the production of duality;
for it is not accepted that a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) arises at the very moment of the production of duality and other such qualities. [Regarding] the specific quality...
It should be understood that this is because, having accepted the absence of obstruction due to being delimited by each successive moment,
it is possible not to accept it in the second moment. Nor should it be argued that, even so,
there would be the impossibility of the destruction of specific qualities produced at the time immediately preceding deep sleep.

In that case, it must be admitted that the very thing itself, as qualified by its own occurrence at a subsequent moment, is the destroyer [of itself]. It should be understood that if destruction were caused everywhere simply by occurring at a subsequent moment, then the existence of *apekṣābuddhi* (the enumerative cognition) for three moments would be untenable. However, in the present context...

The state of being subsequent to itself is simply the state of occurring in the moment that is the locus of its own destruction. Thus, even if one accepts [destruction] as having the relation of inherence (samavāya) with respect to its cause of destruction, there is no deficiency in not postulating it as an obstructer; rather, there is parsimony (lāghava).
Regarding the phrase "by means of being far removed from evil": thus, liberation is indeed the destruction of sin (*pāpa*) alone, and not the destruction of suffering (*duḥkha*);

therefore, the aforementioned logical inconsistency does not apply. Now, one might object: since sin is also a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self, its destruction is possible through a subsequent quality produced immediately after it; so how can the destruction of sin [be the cause of liberation]?

In order to dispel the doubt that [the destruction of demerit] is to be accomplished by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), [the author] introduces "fitness" (*yogyatā*) into the defining characteristic of what is to be destroyed (*nāśyatāvacchedaka*), thereby precluding the possibility of its being destroyed by a subsequent quality (*guṇa*). This is expressed in the words: "And of demerit... (*duritasya ca*). Nor is there any contradiction in the fact that sin is destroyed by a subsequent quality; [this is explained in] the *Rāmarudrī*.
It should not be argued that the inclusion of "fitness" (*yogyatā*) within the delimiting condition (*nāśyatāvacchedakakoṭi*) for destruction by the performance of a desired sacrifice is redundant;
for if that were the case, it would contradict the Vedic scripture which teaches that sin is destroyed by expiation (*prāyaścitta*). This is the intended meaning. Nor is this so...

It should not be argued that since sin is destroyed even by expiation (*prāyaścitta*), knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) cannot be the cause for liberation, because there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)— namely, that [knowledge] does not exist when there is the destruction of sin produced by expiation.
For it is precisely to avoid such a deviation that [the qualification is added].

This is because the form of "extremity" (*ātyantikatva*), consisting in being co-locative with all [one's] own [past] sins and being simultaneous with them, has been included within the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the effect. And it is not the case that, in this way, true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) is not the instrumental cause (*prayojaka*) for the destruction of sin; rather, [it is].

It should not be argued that this is no different from the view of the ancients, [who held] that [the result] consists precisely in being non-simultaneous with the evil (durita) that is co-located with and qualifies that [merit]; for, since individual instances of destruction (dhvaṃsa-vyakti) are mutually distinct, [this applies] to the specific instance of the destruction of sin produced by expiation (prāyaścitta).

The point is that even though it is impossible for [the destruction of a particular instance of suffering] to be produced by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there is no contradiction in its being produced by the knowledge of reality with respect to the specific instance of the destruction of sin immediately following the knowledge of reality. Even if this were the case,

although it would be impossible for the knowledge of reality to produce the destruction of a particular instance of suffering that occurs after the knowledge of reality has ceased, [there is no fault].

Since it is possible for that [liberation] to be produced by the knowledge of reality when it manifests subsequently to such knowledge, there is no fault even in the view of the ancients; nevertheless, it was stated "they say" because of a lack of satisfaction with this [position]. And thus, even if liberation were the destruction of suffering (*duḥkhadhvaṃsa*), there is no inconsistency according to the aforementioned method; therefore, regarding the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*)—

It should be understood that there is no inconsistency [in the author's position], as the author himself indicated through the phrase "the moderns' conceptualization of the definition of demerit (durita) is merely a false construction," which suggests his own dissatisfaction with it. Furthermore, since the Smṛti text— "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes"— teaches that demerit is destroyed by knowledge, [the objection is addressed].

If it is argued that while liberation in the form of the destruction of evil can indeed be accepted as being achievable through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), such a status is not possible for the destruction of suffering because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to indicate that it is produced by the knowledge of reality—even here [in our system], it is said: "Only by knowing Him does one transcend death; there is no other path."

Since the very scripture stating "it exists for the sake of crossing over" can serve as the authority, and because the cessation of absolute suffering alone constitutes the meaning of the term *atyantamṛtyu*,
[it follows that] just as the manifestations of suffering subsequent to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) are destroyed by its own direct perception after that knowledge has arisen, so too...

Since it must be accepted that even those specific instances of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma are destroyed only through experience, there is no distinction [between them and other karmas]; therefore, by the force of scripture alone, it is possible to establish that the destruction of specific suffering is achievable through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Furthermore, [this applies] to the destruction of all karma whatsoever.

Because it is produced by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and because it is awakened [as such] through memory, even the destruction of a merit that is not contemporaneous with a merit residing in the same locus (the self) would result in the undesirable consequence of being liberation (*mukti*). Nor is this a desired consequence, for it lacks the nature of pleasure, the absence of pain, or that which produces them, and thus is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); so, enough of this.

By "pallavitena" (elaborated). Regarding "parityāgarūpā" (of the nature of abandonment): the meaning is that the abandonment of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth is precisely the absence of establishing the thesis as a thesis; thus, its nature is that of a negation (*abhāva*).
Regarding "pratijñātārtha" (the matter proposed): this means the probandum (*sādhya*). Regarding "sādhyāpalāpa" (the denial of the probandum): [this refers to the same].

The meaning is that the denial of the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply its non-statement as something to be proven. Regarding the term "non-expressive" (*avācaka*): it means such things as *huṃ*, *ṭhaḥ*, *phaṭ*, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "non-expressive sentence": here, "expressiveness" (*vācakatva*) consists solely in the capacity to generate cognition, and not in [denotative] power (*śakti*), because that [power] is absent in a sentence; such is the case.
The phrase beginning with "the sentence 'the earth is a breast, the letter *ha* is a medicine,' etc. refers to that which is composed of words with non-established meanings;

the meaning is that it is an instance of the "meaningless" (*apārthaka*). [The example] "the mountain is the locus of fire" and so forth is an instance of the "meaningless. [From the commentary: "impossible at another time," etc.

The meaning is: consisting of the protection of one's wife, children, and so forth. "Interruption of discourse" means the absence of the utterance of words. "Of the tenet" means of the object established in the systems of the logicians (*tārkika*) and others.
"Accepted" means accepted by oneself as something to be proven. "Departure" [from that].
The sense is that it is non-origination (*anupapādanam*), and thus its nature is that of non-existence (*abhāva*). Regarding the suspicion that this might be due to the status of a seer (*ārṣatvam*):

since the author of the *Bhāṣya* is a great seer (*maharṣi*), according to the saying, "As fire consumes everything, so for the luminous ones there is no fault," the presentation of an untenable meaning does not [constitute a flaw].

The sense is that the author of the Muktāvalī has stated that even the modern author of the Maṇi intends to convey such a meaning by the word "doṣayet. Regarding the phrase "among the six categories":
potency (śakti) is not included within substance (dravya), because it is devoid of touch (sparśa).

It is not included among the four beginning with earth, because they possess origination and destruction; nor is it included among the five beginning with space, because it is not contained therein; nor is it included among quality or action, because it resides in qualities, as in the case of the color and other attributes of potsherds and the like.

This is because the capacity to produce the form of a jar and so forth exists [in the clay]; nor does it apply to universals, particulars, or inherence, because they do not possess the nature of arising and perishing—this is the meaning. "Being over-abundant" means being distinct from the seven categories; and it is not the case that... [of it].

It should not be argued that [this category] is included within "non-existence" (abhāva) because it is possible for it to be subsumed there, and thus how could it be distinct from the seven categories?

The point is that it is not included even within non-existence, because it is not the object of a cognition in which a negative particle (*nañ*) is expressed, and because one does not experience it as having a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). In reality, however, [it is said to be] among the six types of non-existence...

The reading [you provide] is merely careless, for by that much alone it is not established that [the object in question] is distinct from the seven categories; furthermore, since adding another reason would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), it is more appropriate to state simply "among the established categories. This is just as [one might argue] that [something] does not exist among eternal substances and so forth, on the grounds that it possesses origination and destruction.
It should be understood that just as there is no inclusion [of capacity] within [the categories], the same applies to eternal absence (*nityābhāva*) and mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*);
for they cannot be included within destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), since it is characterized by perishability, nor within prior absence (*prāgabhāva*), since it is characterized by having come into being.
"Or the transformation of form" means "or the destruction of form."

Simplicity itself is the reason for following the subsequent alternative. Now, one might object that the statement in the root text—that "it is not produced because of its absence"—is redundant, since it does not prove that [the absence] acts as an obstacle.
Therefore, he establishes its purposefulness by demonstrating that it refutes the view that obstacles other than the jewel [are required].

"Distinct from the jewel and so forth" means that space (*gagana*) and other such entities possess the nature of an obstacle (*pratibandhakatva*). And thus, if space and others were the obstacles, then even in a state devoid of a jewel, burning would not occur due to the presence of an obstacle; therefore, the jewel and so forth alone possess the status of being the obstacle.

The sense is that this is the intended meaning of the root text, namely, "it should be stated. "By the reasoning previously stated" means by the reasoning previously stated by himself, beginning with "when there is the presence of a magnet and so forth.
"Even though it is the delimiting factor of causality" refers to [the property] of fire being fire-ness, or [the property] of power being power-ness.

The sense is that fire is not the cause [of burning] by virtue of possessing a power residing in it, because it is cumbersome (gaurava) to posit power as the cause of burning, and because it is more appropriate to posit fire as the cause only when it is qualified by a specific power; thus, power lacks the status of being a cause. In reality, according to the Mīmāṃsakas, with respect to a jar or other effects, there exists in their respective causes a power conducive to the jar and so forth.

It should be understood that this view is also parsimonious (*lāghava*), because by postulating that the status of being a cause belongs solely to the possession of such a specific power (*vilakṣaṇa-śakti*), there is no multiplicity of causalities even due to the differences between the staff, the wheel, and so forth.
This is the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*): because [the effect] arises even when only one of the two—either the removal of the stimulant or the gem—is present.

The sense is that it is impossible for those two [the jewel and the absence of the jewel] in combination to be the cause of burning. Regarding the phrase "not at the time of the presence of the jewel":

since the prevention of burning at the time of the presence of the jewel is possible through the very fact that the absence of the jewel is the cause, it is not reasonable to postulate the existence of an infinite number of powers and so forth.

This is the state of being. Regarding the phrase "due to conceit": in reality, rather than postulating the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of infinite potencies, [one should consider it] by way of the absence of the gem.
